In summary, our research is concerned with
the determination of metabolite concentrations in the human brain in vivo and the elucidation of their regional distribution and possible functional implications.
the regional distribution of metabolites in the human brain and the influence of age and gender on these concentrations.
the development of a method to measure the concentrations of brain metabolites by quantitative localized proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H‐MRS) in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the regional brain metabolite concentrations are in accordance with the distribution pattern of the respective enzymes and the metabolic processes in the human brain.

the regional distribution of metabolites is in accordance with their known metabolic function, but it is also obvious that the metabolic heterogeneity of the brain has to be taken into account when studying the metabolic changes in disease states.
the distribution patterns of metabolites in the human brain are highly complex and not easily explained by the present state of our knowledge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the regional distribution of brain metabolism as determined by quantitative proton MRS is characterized by a high variability and a strong dependence on the metabolic properties of the investigated region.
N‐acetylated compounds are homogeneously distributed, whereas the other metabolites exhibit a distinct regional distribution pattern.

the regional brain metabolite concentrations are not only determined by the regional neuronal density, but are also influenced by regional metabolic processes, such as energy metabolism, and regional membrane turnover.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regional distribution of metabolites in the brain is not homogeneous.
the distribution pattern of the brain metabolites is not random but is highly specific.
there is a lot more variability in the brain than previously thought.
